strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations in EEG tokenization: non-discrete representations, frequency collapse, and poor scalability
Solid technical approach combining STFT and raw signal patches with thoughtful design choices (e.g., gated patchwise aggregation, removal of positional encodings for non-stationary EEG)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 diverse EEG datasets with consistent improvements (5% balanced accuracy, 9% Cohen's Kappa on TUEV) and 3x parameter reduction
Excellent analysis of learned token quality including novel class-token uniqueness metric, spectral entropy validation, retrieval experiments, and visual interpretability (Figure 5)
Thorough ablation studies validating joint frequency-temporal modeling, masking strategies, vocabulary size, and position embeddings
Strong reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, STFT configurations, proper dataset splits, and five random seeds with std. dev.
Demonstrates ability to enhance existing foundation models (LaBraM integration showing 9% balanced accuracy improvement)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines established components (VQ-VAE, STFT, transformers, masking) for EEG application rather than introducing novel algorithms

Critical gap between motivation and evaluation: claims about generalization and scalability across diverse EEG settings are not experimentally validated—all experiments use single-dataset settings (pretrain and finetune on same dataset)
No cross-dataset generalization experiments despite being core motivation; no evidence that approach works across different channel configurations, missing channels, or variable-channel scenarios

Unresolved fixed-windowing limitation: paper acknowledges that patterns split across windows receive separate tokens but offers no solution, affecting interpretability and potentially performance on variable-duration events
Comparison fairness concerns: uses different preprocessing than LaBraM (16-channel vs. 23-channel montage), making it unclear if improvements stem from tokenization or data pipeline differences
Incomplete interpretability validation: visual inspection limited to 2 classes with 3 examples; lacks systematic mapping between learned tokens and known neurophysiological patterns
Missing computational analysis: no comparison of training time, inference speed, or memory footprint despite clinical deployment implications
Statistical rigor limited: no significance testing (e.g., t-tests); some improvements near error margins (TUAB AUC-PR in Table 1); multiple comparisons without correction
Insufficient sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter choices (masking ratio, transformer depths, frequency band size) despite apparent arbitrariness
Incomplete scalability demonstration: single-channel design is theoretically scalable but lacks experimental validation on variable-channel inputs, sparse configurations, or missing channels

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation that clearly identifies gaps in existing EEG tokenization approaches (segment-based without learned vocabulary, discarding tokens at inference)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four diverse datasets with both single- and multi-dataset pretraining, systematic ablation studies, and cross-device scalability validation on ear-EEG
Consistent empirical improvements across all benchmarks (up to 17% Cohen's Kappa on TUEV) with superior parameter efficiency (1.9M vs 5.8M for LaBraM)
Model-agnostic design successfully integrates with existing foundation models (BIOT, LaBraM) as plug-and-play component, improving performance in 93% of cases
Rigorous token quality analysis including class-token uniqueness, consistency metrics via retrieval experiments, and frequency learning analysis using spectral entropy
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters provided, systematic hyperparameter tuning methodology documented, code promised to be released
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (STFT, VQ-VAE, masked language modeling) without novel methodological or theoretical contributions; core contribution is engineering-level combination rather than conceptual advance

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: LaBraM reproduced with 4 datasets vs. original 2500+ hours pretraining; BIOT reproduced rather than official; EEGPT uses mixed published/author results—making it difficult to isolate tokenization's contribution from training setup differences

Single-channel tokenization design insufficiently justified: device-agnosticism claim could also follow from multi-channel aggregation post-tokenization; ear-EEG validation limited (120 recordings, ~8K samples, 4 channels); no comparison to multi-channel tokenization approaches

Shallow analysis of what tokens actually learn: class-token uniqueness scores extremely low (2.14% TUEV, 1.429% IIIC) with no interpretation of what constitutes 'good' scores; only 6 qualitative examples; authors acknowledge windowing causes pattern splits but don't address it; frequency learning evaluated indirectly

Incomplete masking strategy justification: Table 12 shows temporal masking decreases Cohen's Kappa/F1, with symmetric masking mysteriously recovering performance—no clear explanation for this interaction or training instability

Multiple design choices lack theoretical grounding: why VQ-VAE over other quantization methods; why removing positional embeddings helps (explanation is hand-wavy); vocabulary size ablation shows no monotonic trend with no interpretation; joint modeling validated only by ablation
Modest improvements from foundation model integration: ~4% gains with BIOT/LaBraM (Figure 3) much smaller than standalone improvements, suggesting benefits may plateau with model complexity

Limited cross-domain generalization validation: ear-EEG experiment uses same task as pretraining; true out-of-domain transfer to different modalities/tasks not tested; missing comparisons to alternative time-frequency representations and quantization schemes
